title: Determination of Design Limits for a Triaxial (0°/60°/120°) Hexagonal Reinforcement System in Simply Supported Two-Way Reinforced Concrete Slabs: Numerical Evidence, Analytical Derivation, Code-Based Constraints, and Predictive Assessment
content: Conventional two-way slab design relies on orthogonal reinforcement families and established strength, serviceability and detailing provisions. This study asks which design limits govern when a triaxial 0°/60°/120° (hexagonal) reinforcement topology is adopted in two-way slabs simply supported on all edges, with the edges free to move horizontally so that the load is carried by flexure alone; compressive membrane (dome) action and lateral restraint are deferred to a subsequent study. Candidate retained-steel states, including 50%, are evaluated through four methods: the S1–S10 nonlinear finite-element matrix (M1), analytical density and spacing relations (M2), code-based constraints (M3) and a bounded predictive layer (M4). The matched resistance ratios of S1–S10 range from 0.957 to 1.028; they compare numerical limit loads reached at or before the onset of cracking and do not establish a steel-reduction factor at ultimate. For equal bar areas, Rρ = 3sO/(2sH), so 50%, 60% and 66.7% retained steel correspond to spacing multipliers of 3.00, 2.50 and 2.25. A yield-line check shows that the triaxial mesh is isotropic in flexure but no more efficient than an orthogonal mesh (η = 1). In a benchmark series of 6.0 m square simply supported panels (h = 170–400 mm) the governing retained-steel factor is therefore k = 1 at every thickness; even an assumed efficiency η = 1.5 would permit at most an 6% reduction at h = 170 mm and none from h = 195 mm, where minimum reinforcement controls the conventional design. The design limit is formulated as the intersection of all applicable constraints and presented as a code-style, teaching-oriented procedure with worked examples.
